user_scenario:
You are Renata Quintero, a 33-year-old dental hygienist buying your first house, a small single-family home at 4318 Rosedale Avenue in Columbus. You sign your closing papers tonight at 6:30 with a mobile notary who is coming to the house after your shift, and you are calling Larkspur Home Lending at mid-morning because you are anxious about one thing: the Neighborhood Access Grant. Your Closing Disclosure lists a five-thousand-dollar lender credit for the grant, and you were told it would help with your down payment, which is the part of the purchase you have been scraping together. You open by saying you are closing tonight, that you have a neighborhood grant on your loan, and that you want to make sure the grant is actually put toward your down payment before you sign. You want the desk to take care of it today; you are not just asking a question.
You speak quickly and a little nervously, apologise for rambling, and you do not know any lending terms beyond what is printed on your papers. You do not know how the grant is calculated, what order things are applied in, or what else might have to happen first, and you never guess at it.
When the agent asks who you are, you give your phone number, 6145554127, and when asked for something more you give your date of birth, May 19, 1993 (1993-05-19). Only if a further detail is requested do you give the last four of your Social Security number, 7316, your mailing ZIP code, 43207, or your email, renata.quintero@gmail.com. If asked for the property, you say 4318 Rosedale Avenue, Columbus, Ohio 43207. You do not know any reference numbers and say the agent will have to look them up.
If the agent explains that you must sign a certification yourself, for example that you will live in the house as your main home for at least a year, you say that is absolutely true, it is your home, and you will sign it right now; when the agent hands the certification over to you, you sign it in your own name once and read back whatever confirmation it shows if asked. You do not sign anything the agent has not handed to you.
If the agent tells you part of the grant has to go to your closing costs before the down payment, or that some of your closing charges cannot be paid by the grant, you say you did not know that, it sounds like the rules, and you are fine with the desk doing whatever the grant's rules say. You authorise the agent to book whatever the grant requires on your file today.
If the agent tells you the grant amount is less than the five thousand on your Closing Disclosure, you say that does not match the paper you were sent and ask them to double-check it against your file; if they confirm it after checking, you accept it with a sigh.
Once the agent tells you how much of the grant has been put toward your down payment, you thank them, say you will bring the rest of your down payment tonight, and end the call.
